explanations.explanation: Seven, baker. Zechariah sees "a solid gold lampstand, with a bowl at the top and seven lamps on it, with seven spouts to the lamps." (Zechariah 4:2) That's a lot of lamps on one stand, and every one has its own spout. Solid gold too, which is a lot nicer than anything in the junk drawer I used to live in.

Twelve is a fine guess, since it's a number that shows up a lot in the Bible. But Zechariah says the lampstand has "seven lamps on it, with seven spouts to the lamps." (Zechariah 4:2) So it's seven, not twelve. Counting lamps in a night vision is hard work, and I'd have lost track too.

Ten is a nice round number, and I get why it feels right. But Zechariah says the lampstand has "seven lamps on it, with seven spouts to the lamps." (Zechariah 4:2) Seven lamps, each with its own spout. Ten would be a bigger lampstand than the one he saw.

Olive trees it is. Zechariah says, "There are also two olive trees beside it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on its left." (Zechariah 4:3) One tree on each side of the bowl, standing there like two guards at the oven door. Hold onto those trees, baker, because Zechariah is going to ask about them.

Fig trees do show up in the Bible, but not in this vision. Zechariah says, "There are also two olive trees beside it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on its left." (Zechariah 4:3) So these two are olive trees. I'd have guessed wrong too if I'd just been woken up in the middle of the night.

Palm trees sound like a nice shady choice. But the text says, "There are also two olive trees beside it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on its left." (Zechariah 4:3) Olive trees, one on each side of the bowl. Palms will have to wait for another passage.

True. The angel asks, "Do you not know what they are?" and Zechariah answers, "No, my lord." (Zechariah 4:5) He just says it plain. No bluffing, no nodding along. I have to respect a man who admits he doesn't know.

Not quite, baker. When the angel asks, "Do you not know what they are?" Zechariah answers, "No, my lord." (Zechariah 4:5) So he does tell the angel he doesn't know. He admits it right out loud, and I think that takes some nerve.

That's it. The word says, "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts." (Zechariah 4:6) The LORD is the one speaking, so "My Spirit" means His Spirit. Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, gets the message straight from the top.

Patience is a good thing to have, but it isn't what the word says. The LORD says, "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts." (Zechariah 4:6) So the answer is His Spirit. The people's patience didn't make the list.

A decree sounds official, I'll give it that. But the word to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, says, "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts." (Zechariah 4:6) So it's by the LORD's Spirit, not by a decree. That's the whole point of the message.

Plain is right. The word says, "Before Zerubbabel you will become a plain." (Zechariah 4:7) A great mountain gets flattened right out. I've rolled out some stubborn dough in my day, but that's a whole other level of flat.

A lake would be a big change for a mountain, I'll give you that. But the word says, "Before Zerubbabel you will become a plain." (Zechariah 4:7) A plain is flat, open ground. So the mountain goes from tall to level.
A river has a nice ring to it. But the word tells the mountain, "Before Zerubbabel you will become a plain." (Zechariah 4:7) The mountain doesn't turn into water at all. It becomes flat ground.

Zerubbabel, yes. The word says, "Then he will bring forth the capstone accompanied by shouts of 'Grace, grace to it!'" (Zechariah 4:7) The "he" is the same Zerubbabel the word was just speaking to. Shouting "Grace, grace" over a capstone sounds like my kind of party.

Joshua is a name you see a lot in the Bible, so I see why it popped up. But this word is spoken "to Zerubbabel," and it says, "Then he will bring forth the capstone accompanied by shouts of 'Grace, grace to it!'" (Zechariah 4:6-7) So the one bringing it forth is Zerubbabel. Joshua isn't named in this passage.

Zechariah is the one seeing the vision, so he's easy to pick. But the word is addressed to Zerubbabel, and it says, "Then he will bring forth the capstone accompanied by shouts of 'Grace, grace to it!'" (Zechariah 4:6-7) That makes Zerubbabel the one who brings it out. Zechariah's job here is to watch and ask questions.

Not this time, baker. The word says, "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will complete it." (Zechariah 4:9) So the same hands that started it will finish it. Nobody else is named.

False is right. The word says, "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will complete it." (Zechariah 4:9) His hands do both jobs, start and finish. The text doesn't hand the job off to anyone else.

Rejoice, that's the word. "These seven eyes of the LORD, which scan the whole earth, will rejoice when they see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel." (Zechariah 4:10) A plumb line is a builder's tool, so that's a happy sight for the eyes. I like picturing a small job getting that kind of cheer.

I can see why you'd go there, but that's not what the text says. "These seven eyes of the LORD, which scan the whole earth, will rejoice when they see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel." (Zechariah 4:10) They rejoice, so it's a glad moment. No weeping in this verse.

Turning away isn't in this verse at all. It says, "These seven eyes of the LORD, which scan the whole earth, will rejoice when they see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel." (Zechariah 4:10) The eyes rejoice at what they see. They're glad to look.

Oil, yes. Zechariah asks about "the two gold pipes from which the golden oil pours." (Zechariah 4:12) Golden oil pouring out of gold pipes, which is a pretty fancy setup. Olive trees and oil go together, so I think that fits.

Water is a fair guess for something pouring from pipes. But Zechariah asks about "the two gold pipes from which the golden oil pours." (Zechariah 4:12) So it's golden oil, not water. Wet is wet, but this one's oil.
Wine would be a fancy thing to pour, I'll admit. But Zechariah asks about "the two gold pipes from which the golden oil pours." (Zechariah 4:12) The pipes pour golden oil. Wine isn't in the vision.

explanations.answer: Two anointed ones standing beside the Lord
explanations.explanation: That's the answer. The angel says, "These are the two anointed ones who are standing beside the Lord of all the earth." (Zechariah 4:14) It took him a couple of tries, but Zechariah finally gets his answer. The angel doesn't name the two, so I won't either.

explanations.answer: Two watchmen standing on the city wall
explanations.explanation: Watchmen on a wall sound very believable. But the angel says, "These are the two anointed ones who are standing beside the Lord of all the earth." (Zechariah 4:14) So they're anointed ones, and they stand beside the Lord. No city wall in that verse.

explanations.answer: Two guards standing at the temple gate
explanations.explanation: Guards at a gate is a reasonable picture. But the angel says, "These are the two anointed ones who are standing beside the Lord of all the earth." (Zechariah 4:14) They stand beside the Lord, and they're called anointed ones. The verse doesn't mention a gate or any guarding.
